label: delta-Hyperbolic Spaces
notes: This chapter, printed pages 398 to 437, introduces Gromov's coarse negative curvature. The single governing idea is that geodesic triangles are uniformly thin. We motivate it as a large-scale shadow of classical negative curvature, robust enough to survive quasi-isometry and to define a class of groups.

label: Thin Triangles
notes: State the slim triangle condition precisely: every side sits in the delta-neighbourhood of the union of the other two. Stress that delta is a single uniform constant for the whole space, not a local bound. Walk the diagram so students see why a fat Euclidean triangle fails for any fixed delta.

label: Trees as the delta = 0 Case
notes: Trees realise the extreme delta equals zero: triangles degenerate to tripods, so each side already lies on the union of the others. Use this limit to anchor intuition, then describe hyperbolic spaces as spaces that look tree-like at large scale up to the slack delta.

label: The Gromov Product
notes: Introduce the Gromov product as the overlap length of geodesics from a basepoint, measuring how long two rays travel together. Give the formula and the picture of the internal point of a tripod. This scalar repackages the metric and prepares the four-point reformulation of hyperbolicity.

label: Four-Point Condition
notes: Present the four-point inequality: the larger two of three pairwise sums differ by at most two delta. Emphasise that it needs no geodesics, only the metric, so it transfers to arbitrary metric spaces. Note the constants change but the class of hyperbolic spaces does not.

label: Quasi-Geodesics
notes: Define quasi-geodesics with multiplicative and additive constants, allowing controlled detours and discontinuity. Contrast with genuine geodesics. Motivate them as what you actually get from a quasi-isometry, so any invariance theorem must tolerate this coarse, lattice-like sampling of a path rather than exact arc length.

label: The Morse Lemma
notes: State stability of quasi-geodesics: in a hyperbolic space a quasi-geodesic stays within a bounded Hausdorff distance R of a genuine geodesic joining its endpoints, with R depending only on delta and the quasi-geodesic constants. This rigidity is the technical engine of the whole theory.

label: Quasi-Isometry Invariance
notes: Explain why the Morse lemma forces hyperbolicity to be a quasi-isometry invariant: a quasi-isometry carries geodesics to quasi-geodesics, which the lemma straightens, transporting thin triangles across. Hence hyperbolicity is a property of the coarse space, justifying the notion of a hyperbolic group via its Cayley graph.

label: Hyperbolic Groups
notes: A finitely generated group is hyperbolic when some Cayley graph is hyperbolic; invariance makes this independent of the generating set. State the linear isoperimetric inequality characterisation and the consequences: solvable word and conjugacy problems through Dehn's algorithm and bounded conjugator length.

label: Boundary at Infinity
notes: Construct the Gromov boundary as equivalence classes of geodesic rays, or sequences with Gromov product diverging. It is compact and metrizable, and the group acts on it by homeomorphisms. This boundary records the asymptotic directions and is itself a quasi-isometry invariant of the space.

label: Visual Metric
notes: Equip the boundary with a visual metric where distance decays exponentially in the Gromov product of two endpoints. Quasi-isometries induce quasi-symmetric maps of the boundary, so the conformal gauge is the real invariant. Mention the parameter epsilon controlling the exponential and the resulting metric family.

label: Examples and Recap
notes: Close with the canonical examples: trees, real hyperbolic space, and fundamental groups of closed negatively curved manifolds acting cocompactly. Recap the logical spine: thin triangles, Gromov product, four points, Morse stability, invariance, groups, and boundary. Point students to the notebook's slim-triangle and filling experiments.
